issues.legal_issue: A civil court’s jurisdiction to decide a dispute over the educational agency of a private school is not ousted when the statutory scheme does not assign that dispute exclusively to an administrative authority and provides for its determination by a civil court.
material_facts: The suit sought, among other reliefs, a declaration that the plaintiff society was the educational agency for private schools.

The governing statute provided that a dispute about the educational agency of a private school could be decided by a civil court, while excluding civil-court jurisdiction only over questions assigned under the statute to an authority or officer.
The dispute about which party was the educational agency was not one assigned to an administrative authority for decision.
issues.conclusion: Sections 53 and 53A did not oust the civil court’s jurisdiction over the dispute, and the dispute could be brought before it by filing a suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 53 and 53A of the Tamil Nadu Recognized Private Schools (Regulation) Act, 1973, Section 53 excludes civil-court jurisdiction only for questions the Act requires an authority or officer to decide, while Section 53A provides for civil-court determination of disputes about an educational agency. The reference language in Section 53A does not require the parties to make a joint or prior reference before a suit can be filed. Civil-court jurisdiction is not readily inferred to be excluded; the principles in Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh and the cases following it require an express or necessarily implied exclusion.

predicates.private_school_agency_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over which person or body is the educational agency of a private school.
predicates.statutory_scheme_does_not_assign_dispute: The governing statutory scheme does not require an administrative authority to decide the educational-agency dispute exclusively and provides for its decision by a civil court.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the educational agency of a private school and the statutory scheme does not assign that dispute exclusively to an authority, civil-court jurisdiction is not ousted.

issues.legal_issue: A final decision by a competent court on an issue directly and substantially in dispute between parties or their privies bars that issue from being relitigated in a later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier suit, the first appellant and another plaintiff claimed ownership of educational institutions and asserted that they, rather than the respondent society, were their educational agency.

The earlier proceedings determined that the respondent society was the educational agency and owner of the relevant institutions, that the first appellant acted as its agent, and that the second appellant trust did not exist as a legally constituted trust.
The earlier decision was affirmed through the appellate proceedings and became final.
The later suit concerned the parties’ claims to the same institutions, properties, and educational-agency status.
The civil court had jurisdiction to decide the earlier dispute.
issues.conclusion: The findings in the earlier proceedings were binding in the later suit under the doctrine of res judicata, and the appellants could not reopen the matters already determined.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule that an issue directly and substantially decided by a competent court between the same parties or their privies cannot be tried again in subsequent litigation. The rule promotes finality and prevents repeated litigation. The Court relied on Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, and Ishwardas v. State of Madhya Pradesh. A judgment of a court lacking inherent jurisdiction would be a nullity and would not create a res judicata bar, but the earlier court had jurisdiction here.

rule.if: later_civil_suit and prior_final_judgment_by_competent_court and same_parties_or_privies and same_issue_directly_and_substantially_decided

predicates.later_civil_suit: A civil suit is brought after an earlier proceeding between the relevant parties or their privies.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_by_competent_court: A court with jurisdiction has issued a final judgment in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The parties to the later proceeding are the same as, or claim through, parties to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_and_substantially_de: The issue sought to be raised again was directly and substantially in dispute and was decided in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: When a later civil suit involves the same parties or their privies and seeks to relitigate an issue finally decided by a competent court, that issue is barred from relitigation.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to frame a separate issue on res judicata does not invalidate a decision when the plea was sufficiently raised, the parties understood and litigated it, and the omission caused no prejudice.
material_facts: The plaintiff society’s pleading extensively referred to the earlier litigation and asserted that its findings barred the appellants’ claims.
The appellants responded to the earlier proceedings in their pleadings and acknowledged that the pending appeal concerned matters material to the later suit.
The parties placed the relevant pleadings, documents, and earlier judgments before the trial court and litigated the matters underlying the res judicata plea.
The appellants did not object to the plea at trial, and the Court found that they had adequate opportunity to meet it and had suffered no prejudice from the absence of a separately framed issue.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a separately framed issue on res judicata did not prevent the court from applying the doctrine or invalidate its decision.
issues.legal_principle: A res judicata plea should ordinarily be founded in the pleadings and addressed by an issue, as explained in V. Rajeshwari v. T.C. Saravanabava. However, the omission is not fatal where the relevant facts were before the parties and court, the parties went to trial knowing the real issue and had an opportunity to adduce evidence, and no prejudice resulted. The Court relied on the exception discussed in V. Rajeshwari and on Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao; it also referred to Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar on the effect of litigating an issue with full knowledge of it.

rule.if: civil_trial and res_judicata_pleaded_in_substance and parties_knew_issue_at_trial and relevant_evidence_adduced and no_prejudice_from_omission

predicates.civil_trial: The proceeding is a civil trial in which the court is asked to decide whether an earlier judgment bars a claim or issue.
predicates.res_judicata_pleaded_in_substance: A party’s pleadings set out the earlier proceeding and assert that its determination bars the matter in the current proceeding.
predicates.parties_knew_issue_at_trial: The parties understood that the effect of the earlier judgment was a matter to be determined at trial.
predicates.relevant_evidence_adduced: The parties put before the court the relevant earlier pleadings, judgments, or other evidence concerning the asserted bar.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_omission: The party opposing the bar had an adequate opportunity to meet it and was not disadvantaged by the failure to frame a separate issue.

issues.definition: In a civil trial, failure to frame a separate issue on res judicata does not invalidate the decision when the plea was raised in substance, the parties understood and litigated it with relevant evidence, and the omission caused no prejudice.
